candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body: At the end of the year, the Profit and Loss Account of a partnership firm shows a credit balance (net profit). Which journal entry transfers this balance to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account?

options.text: Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c Dr. To Profit and Loss A/c
Profit and Loss A/c Dr. To Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c
Profit and Loss A/c Dr. To Interest on Capital A/c
Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c Dr. To Partners' Capital A/c

candidate.explanation: For a credit balance (net profit) the entry given is Profit and Loss A/c Dr. To Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c. Option A is the entry given for a debit balance (net loss), so it does not fit a net profit. Options C and D credit a different account, whereas the entry given for transferring the balance credits the Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c.

learning_objective.objective: Record the transfer of the Profit and Loss Account balance to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account.

candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body: P and Q are partners who admit R with a guarantee that R's share of profit will not be less than Rs. 30,000. The guarantee is given by P and Q, who will bear any shortfall in the ratio 3:2. The firm's profit for the year is Rs. 1,50,000 and the profit sharing ratio of P, Q and R is 3:2:1. What amount of profit will P finally get?
candidate.explanation: R's share by the ratio is 1/6 of Rs. 1,50,000 = Rs. 25,000, which is Rs. 5,000 less than the guaranteed Rs. 30,000, so the shortfall is borne by the guaranteeing partners. P's share by the ratio is 3/6 of Rs. 1,50,000 = Rs. 75,000 and P bears 3/5 of Rs. 5,000 = Rs. 3,000, so P gets Rs. 72,000. Rs. 75,000 ignores the shortfall, Rs. 73,000 deducts 2/5 of Rs. 5,000 (Rs. 2,000), and Rs. 70,000 deducts the whole Rs. 5,000.

learning_objective.objective: Compute partners' shares of profit when a new partner is given a guarantee of minimum profit.

candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body: A and B share profits in the ratio 2:1. C is admitted for 1/4 share of profits and brings in Rs. 20,000 as his capital. The remaining 3/4 share is divided between A and B in their old ratio 2:1. After all adjustments, the capitals of A and B are Rs. 45,000 and Rs. 15,000, and it is agreed that the capitals of the partners will be in proportion to their new profit shares, the total capital of the new firm being Rs. 80,000. What adjustment is needed in B's capital?

options.text: B withdraws Rs. 5,000
B brings in Rs. 20,000
B brings in Rs. 5,000
No adjustment is needed

candidate.explanation: B's new share is 1/3 of the remaining 3/4, i.e. 1/4, so B's required capital is 1/4 of Rs. 80,000 = Rs. 20,000. B's capital is Rs. 15,000, which is Rs. 5,000 short, so B must bring in Rs. 5,000. Withdrawing Rs. 5,000 would apply to a surplus, which B does not have; Rs. 20,000 is the required capital, not the shortfall; and no adjustment is wrong because B's capital of Rs. 15,000 differs from Rs. 20,000.

learning_objective.objective: Adjust old partners' capitals to be proportionate to the new profit sharing ratio on admission of a partner.

candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body: A firm has capital employed of Rs. 3,00,000 and the normal rate of return is 10%. Its average profit is Rs. 45,000. Using the capitalisation of super profit method, with Normal Profit = Capital Employed x Normal Rate/100 and Goodwill = Super Profit x 100/Normal Rate of Return, what is the value of goodwill?
candidate.explanation: Normal Profit = Rs. 3,00,000 x 10/100 = Rs. 30,000 and Super Profit = Rs. 45,000 - Rs. 30,000 = Rs. 15,000. Goodwill = Rs. 15,000 x 100/10 = Rs. 1,50,000. Rs. 15,000 is only the super profit, Rs. 4,50,000 is average profit x 100/10, and Rs. 30,000 is the normal profit; none of these is Super Profit x 100/10.

learning_objective.objective: Value goodwill by the capitalisation of super profit method.

candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body: A company earned no profit in a year. Which statement about its obligations towards debentureholders is correct?

options.text: Interest on debentures is a charge on profits and is to be paid even if there is no profit
Interest on debentures is an appropriation of profits and need not be paid when there is no profit
Interest on debentures varies from year to year with the profits of the company
Interest on debentures is payable only if debentureholders exercise voting rights

candidate.explanation: The payment of interest is a charge on profits and is to be paid even if there is no profit. Option B is wrong because it is the payment of dividend that is an appropriation of profits. Option C is wrong because the rate of interest on debentures is prefixed, while the rate of return on shares may vary with profits. Option D is wrong because debentureholders do not normally enjoy voting rights and the payment of interest is not tied to them.

learning_objective.objective: Distinguish debentures from shares in respect of the nature of return.

candidate.subject: business_studies
candidate.body: Using the definitions by Chester Barnard and Keith Davis, which statement about an informal organisation is correct?

It exists only when its relationships contribute to joint results
It is created through a conscious purpose set by management
It arises spontaneously as people associate with one another, without being established or required by the formal organisation

The overall cost of capital is likely to fall, but fixed financial charges and financial risk increase

candidate.subject: business_studies

options.text: Rs 17,200; a combination of time based pay plus incentive for higher performance

Rs 17,200; an indirect payment like employer paid insurance

candidate.chapter: Theory of Firms under Perfect Competition
candidate.body: A wheat farmer in a perfectly competitive market is a price-taking firm and sells every unit at the market price of Rs 40 per quintal. If she sells one more quintal, her marginal revenue from that extra quintal is:

options.text: Less than Rs 40, because she must lower the price to sell the extra quintal
Rs 0, because the extra quintal is sold at the same price as the earlier ones
Rs 40, because the extra unit is sold at the market price
Rs 40 multiplied by her total output, because all units are sold at that price

candidate.explanation: For a price-taking firm, the extra unit is sold at the market price, so marginal revenue is precisely the market price, i.e. MR = AR = p = Rs 40. The firm does not need to lower its price, so MR is not below Rs 40. The extra quintal adds Rs 40 to revenue, so MR is not zero or Rs 40 times total output.

learning_objective.objective: Explain that for a perfectly competitive firm marginal revenue equals the market price

candidate.subject: economics
candidate.body: At an output of 4 units, a firm has a total fixed cost of Rs 80 and a total variable cost of Rs 120. Using SAC = AVC + AFC, what is the short run average cost (SAC) at 4 units?

options.text: Rs 30
Rs 50
Rs 200
Rs 20

candidate.explanation: AFC is obtained by dividing fixed cost by output (80/4 = Rs 20) and AVC by dividing variable cost by output (120/4 = Rs 30). Since SAC = AVC + AFC, SAC = 30 + 20 = Rs 50. Rs 30 is only AVC and Rs 20 is only AFC; Rs 200 is the total of 80 + 120, not a per-unit cost.

candidate.body: A person invests Rs 2,00,000 in her family business. The alternatives she could have chosen were: keeping the money in a house-safe (zero return), depositing it in bank-1 at 10 per cent interest per year, or depositing it in bank-2 at 5 per cent interest per year. She can use the money in only one of these ways. The opportunity cost per year of investing in the family business is:

options.text: Rs 0

candidate.explanation: The maximum benefit from the other alternatives is the interest from bank-1, and the opportunity cost of the family business is that forgone interest. 10 per cent of Rs 2,00,000 is Rs 20,000. Bank-2 gives only Rs 10,000, which is not the best alternative; the safe gives zero; and since the alternatives are either/or, their returns are not added to Rs 30,000.

learning_objective.objective: Compute opportunity cost as the forgone return of the best alternative use of funds

candidate.subject: economics
candidate.body: Government spending on domestic goods rises in an open economy where a proportion of the induced increase in consumption is spent on imported goods. Compared with a closed economy in which all induced consumption is spent on domestic goods, the autonomous expenditure multiplier in this open economy is:

options.text: Larger, because imported goods add to domestic income at each round
Unchanged, because only the change in autonomous expenditure matters
Smaller, because the induced effect on demand for domestic goods is smaller
Smaller or larger depending on the size of the government spending

candidate.explanation: With a positive mpc, part of the induced consumption becomes demand for foreign, not domestic, goods. So the induced effect on domestic income is smaller, and imports per unit of income are an additional leakage at each round that reduces the value of the multiplier. It is therefore not larger or unchanged, and nothing in the stem or excerpt links the size of spending to the direction of the change.

learning_objective.objective: Explain how imports act as a leakage that reduces the autonomous expenditure multiplier

candidate.subject: economics
candidate.body: A farmer's four-acre farm needs only two workers and himself to carry out its operations through the year. He employs five workers along with his wife and children, and everyone on the farm works throughout the year. This situation is best described as:

options.text: Disguised unemployment, because more persons are employed than the farm actually needs
Open unemployment, because the extra persons have no work at all and are seeking jobs
Seasonal unemployment, because farm work is available only in some months of the year
Full employment, because every person on the farm is working

candidate.explanation: The farm needs only two workers and the farmer, yet employs five workers plus family members; this situation is known as disguised unemployment. It is not open unemployment since the stem says everyone on the farm works, and not seasonal since they work throughout the year. Full employment is contradicted by the excerpt, which labels this very situation disguised unemployment.
